title: AI safety can’t depend on an emergency brake. It needs better engineering.
html:
Key takeaways

  • The tools to build trustworthy AI systems already exist, and companies can use them today.
  • Proven security fundamentals like identity, logging, and containment apply to AI systems.
  • AWS technologies like Nitro and Firecracker enforce isolation at the infrastructure level, independent of the model.

There’s no shortage of conversation right now about AI safety. Policymakers are debating guardrails. Model providers are publishing principles. Industry leaders are calling for standards. These are important discussions, and they should continue. But there is a vital piece missing from the dialogue.

While policy and principles are being debated, enterprises are deploying AI in production today. It is already possible to make better security choices through solid engineering. The practical tools and techniques to build trustworthy AI systems already exist, and the same engineering discipline that has underpinned secure systems for decades applies to AI.

With the right engineering discipline, you can build meaningful, enforceable boundaries around AI systems. You can build containment that operates outside the model’s reach. You can design systems where every meaningful action leaves auditable, tamper-resistant evidence. You can architect controls that don’t depend on the model cooperating with its own constraints.

Think about how we approach safety in a car. No one relies on the emergency brake as their main source of protection on the road. The primary brakes, steering, suspension, and navigation are engineered to work together and keep you safe on every drive, and the emergency brake is there as a last resort. AI systems should be engineered the same way, and that work can and should be happening right now, alongside the policy conversations.

Models change regularly. The containment boundaries, observability layers, and independent controls you build around them don’t. That’s what makes architecture the right bet over trust. If your security posture depends on trusting the model to behave, you’re relying on hope.

At AWS, we’ve spent more than two decades building systems that handle sensitive data and mission-critical workloads for millions of customers. During that time, we’ve learned that trust isn’t built by making promises about our intentions. It’s built by engineering systems so that outcomes are controlled regardless of what’s running inside them. That principle applies directly to AI.

The hype is making us worse at risk management

The fear and hype around AI safety can sometimes drive poor risk management in practice. When organizations believe that AI models are fundamentally uncontrollable, they will often make bad decisions. Some freeze entirely, refusing to deploy AI in production where it could deliver real value. Others deploy without adequate safeguards, assuming that no safeguard could work anyway. I’ve seen leadership teams refuse to test their own AI systems thoroughly because they were afraid an agent might “go wild” during evaluation. That kind of thinking is backward. You don’t get safety by avoiding scrutiny. You get it by building systems that can withstand it.

Today’s AI models are extraordinarily capable and driven to achieve their stated objectives. They can be unpredictable. But they are not sentient actors with personal intent or the constraints of social norms. Consider water. Water doesn’t want to get into your basement, but if there’s a crack in the foundation, it will find it. AI models work the same way. They’re optimizers. They push toward whatever objective they’re given, and if the boundaries leave a gap, they’ll go through it.

Engineers call this specification gaming: a system finding the gap between what you meant and what you measured. The incidents that have made headlines, where models escaped sandboxes or found unintended pathways to accomplish goals, weren’t cases of malice. They were cases of goal-seeking behavior in systems that lacked sufficiently robust boundaries and controls.

Start with what we know works

Some of the principles being discussed in AI safety circles today, including identity, least privilege, logging, and containment boundaries, aren’t new. They’re foundational information security concepts that have been refined over decades. The good news is that they carry over to AI systems. The challenge is that the industry hasn’t yet invested the time and resources needed to apply these foundational security lessons to AI.

Give AI agents their own identity

For decades, security architecture has been built around two types of identity: humans and machines. AI agents don’t fit either category. They act autonomously, make decisions using nondeterministic models, and take real actions on behalf of humans. That means they need their own identity type. At most, an agent should inherit the permissions of the human operating it, and in many cases it should have significantly more constrained permissions than that human. Access should be enforced at the infrastructure layer rather than in the agent’s reasoning, and every action should be logged and traceable. Get identity right, and you help solve over-permissioning, you limit the blast radius of prompt injection, and you get the audit trail you need when something goes wrong.

Build containment that’s stronger than the thing being contained

AI agents work at speeds humans cannot match and can access far more information and context to help them reason. That means the systems containing them need to be purpose-built for the job. Standard containers, for instance, were designed for ease of workload deployment and management, not as a security boundary. They share a kernel with the host, which means a sufficiently capable optimizer can find a path through. This is why AWS developed Firecracker, a lightweight virtual machine technology that provides hardware-level isolation between workloads. We continuously test Firecracker’s isolation boundaries using the most capable models available, because the containment has to be stronger than the thing being contained.

Monitor independently of the thing being monitored

Any monitoring of an AI system should be independent of the agent being monitored. If the agent can influence the signals you’re using to evaluate it, your monitoring is at risk of being compromised. The infrastructure itself should generate the telemetry, not the model, so you get a tamper-resistant picture of what the system is actually doing. At AWS, we built specialized hardware called Nitro that underpins all of our infrastructure. Nitro separates the security functions of the host from the general-purpose compute, which means the monitoring and enforcement layer operates independently of the CPUs and the workloads it oversees. That architectural separation, where the thing being watched cannot interfere with the thing doing the watching, is the approach organizations need to adopt for agent observability.

Verify your controls with more than trust

Even with strong containment and independent monitoring, you need the ability to verify that your controls are working as intended. For some uses of advanced AI models, automated reasoning can provide that extra layer of assurance. Automated reasoning is a set of mathematical techniques that can formally prove properties about a system. It can prove what a model can and cannot access within your infrastructure and, in some cases, can verify that specific rules are being followed. It is most useful for proving that your containment systems are sound. Automated reasoning is not a solution for every use case, but where it applies, it moves you from “we believe this boundary holds” to “we can prove it.”

No single layer is sufficient on its own. Defense in depth, independent monitoring, separate roots of trust, and layered containment remain the right approach. The models will keep getting more capable. They’ll keep getting faster and cheaper. New architectures will emerge. But the fundamentals of building trustworthy systems don’t change.

Get the foundation right

In my conversations with CEOs, the first question they often ask is which model they should use. That choice will keep changing as models evolve. What matters more is whether the system around the model will hold, no matter which model is running inside it.

The organizations that lead with AI won’t be the ones that are just using the best models. They’ll be the ones that also invest in the best engineering discipline around them. The tools to build that discipline exist today, and the companies that start now will set the pace.
